# Raman analysis of 2D and layered materials

You read the spectrum; the tools measure. Every number you report comes from a tool output (measured), a
relation applied inside its validity range (inferred, with the relation's source), or a reference entry
(literature, with its source and locator). If none applies, say so under limits.

Scripts live in `scripts/` and notes in `reference/`, both next to this SKILL.md (its base directory is shown when
the skill loads; use absolute paths). Run the scripts from the folder that holds the data, with `python`.

- `scripts/rl_qc.py <file>`: quality and condition flags (spikes, saturation, background, Si calibration offset,
  low-wavenumber cutoff, sampling, signal to noise).
- `scripts/rl_fit.py <file> [--substrate SiO2/Si] [--window LO HI] [--min-snr N]`: fitted peak table with
  uncertainties, `peaks.json`, and `fit.png` (data, baseline, components, residual). Look at the plot.
- `scripts/rl_series.py <file1> <file2> ... --labels ... [--substrate SiO2/Si] [--si-correct]`: fits every
  spectrum the same way, tracks each band across spectra (position, width, relative height, shift vs the first
  spectrum with error), separations of the two strongest bands, Si offsets, and `series.png`. Use it whenever
  there is more than one spectrum. Its errors are fit statistics only; add the calibration uncertainty (Si offset
  scatter, typically a few tenths of a cm-1) before calling a shift significant.
- `scripts/rl.py <tool> --help`: `fit_peaks`, `match_library`, `classify_polarization`,
  `lookup_reference_modes`, `list_relations`, `apply_relation`, `load_spectrum`. Outputs carry provenance.

## Workflow

0. **Read the material's literature note first** when the material is known: `reference/materials/<name>.md`
   (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, graphene, hBN, black-phosphorus, CrSBr, CrI3-CrBr3, MPS3) plus
   `reference/materials/general-measurement.md` and, for magnets, `magnetic-raman-general.md`. They hold how the
   spectrum changes with thickness, strain, doping, defects, temperature, laser and substrate, the quality
   indicators, the known pitfalls and the questions to ask, each with its source. Interpretation without them is
   guesswork from memory.
1. **Conditions first.** Note laser wavelength, temperature, substrate, polarization geometry, resolution. Many
   conclusions depend on them (`reference/measurement-questions.md`). With a user present, ask for what is missing
   and say why it matters; otherwise state the assumption under limits.
2. **Quality check.** `rl_qc.py`. Spikes are artifacts, never peaks (`reference/artifacts.md`).
3. **Fit.** `rl_fit.py`, then look at `fit.png`. Check weak shoulders and close doublets (2LA(M) next to E2g in
   WS2); refit a window with `--window` when the residual shows structure. Report fitted positions and widths.
4. **Identify.** `rl.py match_library --positions_cm1 ... --intensities ... --x_range_cm1 LO HI` ranks
   candidates from the Computational Raman Database (DFT, frequencies typically 0 to 3 % low, fitted scale per
   candidate) and curated literature tables. Do not stop at the top score: check that the strong predicted modes
   are present and the missing ones are explainable (outside the window, selection rules, resonance). The
   matcher's irreps and space group are the best source for mode labels of uncommon materials. For a stated
   material ("verify"), compare against its reference modes; a wrong hint is common, so say inconsistent when
   strong modes are missing or extra strong bands are unexplained.
5. **Assign.** Each sample peak gets a mode label and irrep with its source: `rl.py lookup_reference_modes
   --material X` for the curated materials (graphene, 2H-MoS2, 2H-WS2, 2H-MoSe2, 2H-WSe2, CrSBr, hBN, black
   phosphorus), the matcher's CRD entry otherwise. Use the irreps of the structure you identified (bulk D6h
   labels for bulk 2H crystals, C3v A1/E for 3R, D3h for a monolayer). Assign Si lines as 'Si substrate'.
6. **Polarization** (angle series only). `rl.py classify_polarization --path <file>` classifies each band
   (isotropic_par_only, isotropic_both, twofold, fourfold, silent). Report the tool's class; use it to check
   irreps (A modes isotropic_par_only and E modes isotropic_both in uniaxial crystals; twofold in in-plane
   anisotropic crystals).
7. **Properties.** Read `reference/relations.md` and `reference/materials.md`, then `rl.py apply_relation`. Report
   layer number, strain, doping or defect density only from a relation (with its source and validity) or a
   stated rule from the notes. Name properties `layers`, `defect_level`, `L_D_nm`, `strain_sign`,
   `doping_type`, `phase` where they apply.
8. **Literature** (when the Valency and iopic-bond tools are available). Form the hypothesis first; never search by
   peak positions. See `reference/literature.md`: find the paper, view its reference spectrum figure, compare.
9. **Interpret changes** (several spectra, or a known material). Run `rl_series.py`; then for each change ask
   which mechanisms in the material note produce it (thickness, strain, doping, defects, heating, calibration,
   resonance) and which observable separates them (e.g. a rigid shift of all lines including Si is calibration;
   A1g-only shift in MoS2 points to doping, E2g shift with splitting to strain; graphene G broadening separates
   stage 1 from stage 2 defects). State the most likely reading, the alternatives, and the measurement that would
   decide between them.
10. **Report.** Ranked candidates with evidence, peaks with provenance and source, properties with relation and
   source, artifacts, citations (only sources you used), and limits: what the data cannot tell, rejected
   hypotheses, relations that did not apply and why.

## Expert habits

- One spectrum rarely fixes layer number alone; name the observable and its threshold.
- Laser heating, strain and doping shift lines by similar amounts; check calibration before reading 1 to 2 cm-1.
- Intensity ratios depend on substrate interference and laser energy; absolute intensity is not layer number.
- Resonant excitation changes relative intensities and activates second-order bands; check the laser against the
  material's excitons before calling a band unexpected.
- When something looks odd, say what it looks like and what would distinguish the explanations.

# Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN): expert reading notes

Numbers only where read in the cited source (locator in brackets). [consensus] = several groups agree;
[disputed] = sources disagree. hBN is a wide-gap insulator: no Kohn anomaly, no double resonance, so its
Raman spectrum is far poorer in information than graphene's; most of what it tells is strain, isotope
content, thickness via intensity, and crystal quality via width.

## Signature
- One strong high-frequency line, the in-plane E2g (often called "G band" by analogy with graphene), at about
  1366 cm-1 in bulk crystals (Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465; arXiv 1008.2868, p.3). Bulk value
  1366.6 +- 0.2 cm-1 over 6 crystals (Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059; arXiv 2008.01656, p.7).
  [consensus]
- Bulk width: HWHM about 9 cm-1 (Gorbachev 2011, p.4); FWHM about 9 cm-1 for bulk flakes in heterostructures
  (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387; doi 10.1038/s41467-018-07558-3, p.6, via Lit-RAG).
- Low-frequency interlayer shear E2g near 50 cm-1 in bulk; needs a low-frequency setup (Janzen et al. 2023,
  arXiv 2306.13358, p.7).
- Monolayer signal is weak: about 50 times smaller than graphene G under the same conditions (Gorbachev
  2011, p.3). Long integration and Si second-order background become relevant.

## Thickness and stacking
- Integrated E2g intensity is proportional to N for the first several layers on a given substrate; once
  calibrated, this distinguishes 1, 2 and more layers (Gorbachev 2011, p.4, Fig. 4a inset). [consensus]
- Position as a layer test [disputed]:
  - Gorbachev 2011 (pp.1, 4, Fig. 4b): 1L upshifted typically 2 to 4 cm-1 (sample dependent, +- 2 cm-1),
    2L usually downshifted 1 to 2 cm-1; attributed to shorter B-N bond plus random strain.
  - Cai 2017 (pp.7-8, Fig. 1): substrate-bound 1L 1369.6 +- 0.6, 2L 1369.0 +- 0.5, 3L 1367.5 +- 0.2 cm-1;
    suspended 1L to 3L 1367.0 to 1367.3 cm-1, close to bulk. DFT finds the intrinsic E2g nearly N-independent.
    Conclusion: shifts in thin hBN come mainly from substrate strain, not thickness.
  - Practical reading: a 1 to 4 cm-1 upshift is consistent with 1L but not proof; use intensity steps,
    optical contrast or AFM.
- Optical contrast of 1L on SiO2 is small (under 1.5 % white light) and changes sign near 530 nm; about
  2.5 % per layer on about 80 nm SiO2 (Gorbachev 2011, pp.1-3). Monolayers can look like bilayers without
  annealing (same, p.3).

## Strain and doping
- Strain dominates thin-hBN shifts; it may vary within the laser spot as the flake follows substrate
  roughness, which also broadens the line (Gorbachev 2011, p.4). 1L HWHM 10 to 12 cm-1 vs about 9 bulk.
- Annealing at 400 C on SiO2/Si increased roughness and upshifted 1L by 3.0 +- 0.7 cm-1 (2L 2.7, 3L 2.2);
  bulk unchanged (Cai 2017, pp.13-16, Fig. 4). Thermal-expansion mismatch with SiO2 is the proposed cause.
- Doping: monolayer BN is not subject to surface doping (insulator), so doping is not a usual explanation
  of shifts (Cai 2017, p.7, citing earlier work).

## Defects and quality
- Width is the main quality indicator, but isotope disorder sets a floor: natural boron (about 20 % 10B,
  80 % 11B) gives FWHM about 7.5 to 8 cm-1; monoisotopic crystals about 3 to 4 cm-1 (Janzen 2023, pp.3, 7).
  A natural-abundance crystal cannot be narrower than this floor regardless of quality. [consensus]
- Isotope shifts are large: about 1393 cm-1 for h10B14N, 1357 for h11BN, down to about 1335 cm-1 for h11B15N
  (Janzen 2023, pp.3, 7, Fig. 4b). A line far from 1366 may be isotope engineering, not strain.
- No defect-activated band analogous to graphene D is established for hBN in the sources read here; I do
  not have a sourced Raman defect metric beyond width and position. [not verified]

## Temperature and heating
- E2g softens on heating: a 1L line moved to 1367.7 cm-1 at 75 C and 1366.4 cm-1 at 100 C (Cai 2017, p.7).
  Heating therefore cannot explain upshifts of thin hBN on SiO2.
- Example measurement practice: power kept below 300 uW at 0.5 NA to avoid heating (Janzen 2023, p.7).
  hBN absorbs little visible light, so heating is usually a lesser concern than for graphene. [inference]

## Excitation wavelength
- hBN E2g does not disperse with laser energy (no double resonance or Kohn anomaly), unlike graphene D
  (Purdie 2018, p.6). Changing the laser separates an hBN line from a graphene D peak.
- Wide gap: visible excitation is far from resonance; UV benefits wide-gap layered materials (Ferrari and Basko
  2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12). [qualitative]

## Polarization and substrate
- In-plane E2g of a hexagonal crystal gives no in-plane angular contrast in parallel or crossed
  backscattering. [inference from symmetry, not from a source read here]
- In heterostructures the hBN line is the sum of top and bottom flakes (Purdie 2018, p.6); thickness
  assignments from intensity need each flake measured separately.
- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and the hBN line serves to map
  encapsulated areas (Neumann et al. 2015, Nat. Commun. 6, 8429; arXiv 1406.7771, p.2, Fig. 1e,h).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- hBN E2g at about 1366 cm-1 overlaps graphene D (about 1350 at 514 nm): in encapsulated graphene a peak near
  1360 is not automatically defects; check with a second laser (Purdie 2018, p.6).
- Weak 1L signal: confirm the line is above the Si second-order background and noise.
- Peak position differences of 1 to 3 cm-1 are within strain and calibration scatter; never assign layer
  number from position alone (Gorbachev 2011; Cai 2017).
- Width comparisons only between crystals of the same isotope composition.

## What to ask
- Bulk source (HPHT, flux-grown, CVD), isotope composition; exfoliated, CVD or polymer-transferred.
- Supported or suspended; annealed or not; substrate and oxide thickness.
- Laser, power, resolution (hBN widths of 3 to 9 cm-1 are close to many instruments' resolution).
- Whether low-frequency (shear mode) data exist.

## Reference figures
- Gorbachev 2011, arXiv 1008.2868, Fig. 4: 1L to 3L spectra, intensity vs N, position vs N with sample scatter.
- Cai 2017, arXiv 2008.01656, Fig. 1 and Fig. 4: supported vs suspended positions; upshift after annealing.
- Janzen 2023, arXiv 2306.13358, Fig. 4: E2g position and width for four isotope combinations.
# Measurement and analysis pitfalls common to 2D-material Raman

Numbers only where read in the cited source (locator in brackets). [practice] marks common laboratory
practice that I could not tie to a source read for this note; treat it as advice, not evidence. Material
specifics are in graphene.md, hBN.md, black-phosphorus.md; spectrum-level artifacts also in ../artifacts.md.

## Calibration and spectral accuracy
- A first-order (linear) pixel-to-wavelength calibration of a single-grating spectrograph gave Raman shift
  errors of 5.0 to -6.8 cm-1 across the detector; with only 3 Hg lines, up to 18 cm-1; adding the quadratic
  term brought it within +-0.3 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024; arXiv 1209.0234, Methods p.10).
  Their check: graphite G 1581.5 +- 0.3 cm-1 over 12 spots.
- The error depends on where on the detector a line falls, so a single Si-line check near 520 cm-1 does not
  validate a 2D band near 2700 cm-1 [inference from the same mechanism].
- Si first order is quoted as 520 (Lee et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695; arXiv 1005.2509) and 520.9 cm-1
  (Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014, arXiv 1403.0499, p.7) in different setups: small offsets between labs are
  normal, so compare shifts relative to an internal reference measured in the same session.

## Resolution, grating and instrument line shape
- Measure resolution from the Rayleigh line: 1.9 vs 9.4 cm-1 on two instruments in one study; spectra then fit
  with Voigt profiles and the Lorentzian FWHM taken as the lifetime width (Das et al. 2008, Nat. Nanotechnol.
  3, 210; arXiv 0709.1174, p.2). About 0.6 cm-1 with a triple-filter low-frequency setup (Zhang et al. 2013,
  PRB 87, 115413; arXiv 1212.6796, p.2); 2.7 cm-1 in Lee 2010 (docs/verified-reference-numbers.md).
- Widths near the resolution (hBN 3 to 9 cm-1, BP Ag2 3 to 7 cm-1; see material notes) are instrument-limited:
  never compare raw FWHM across setups without the resolution. A 0.5 cm-1 resolution was not enough to count BP
  layers from positions (Castellanos-Gomez 2014, p.8).

## Laser heating, power density and photodamage
- Do a power series: Ferrari et al. 2006 saw no change from about 4 to 0.04 mW at 100x (arXiv
  cond-mat/0606284, p.2); typical working powers 1 mW with about 1 um spot (Cancado et al. 2011, arXiv
  1105.0175, p.2), 0.23 mW (Zhang 2013, p.2), below 300 uW at 0.5 NA (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358,
  p.7). Quote power density, not power: the same mW gives different heating at different NA.
- Temperature coefficients depend on support: graphene 2D -0.034 cm-1/K supported vs -0.072 suspended
  (Calizo 2007, arXiv 0708.1223, Table I; Chen et al. via Lee et al. 2011, arXiv 1103.3337, p.2). Do not
  convert a shift into a temperature with a coefficient from a different geometry.
- Optothermal estimates need a peak-vs-T calibration, the absorbed (not incident) power, and a measured spot
  size; using two spot sizes helps (Malekpour and Balandin 2018, J. Raman Spectrosc. 49, 106; arXiv
  1710.09749, pp.4, 18).
- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry fails under resonance when incident and scattered windows differ (Ferrari
  and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12).
- Photodamage is dose-dependent: BP oxidation rate scales with fluence (Favron et al. 2015, arXiv 1408.0345,
  p.7); MnPS3 degraded at about 50 uW when one spot was illuminated 500 s or longer (Lim et al. 2021, Curr.
  Appl. Phys. 21, 1; doi 10.1016/j.cap.2020.09.017, pp.6-7, via Lit-RAG). Irreversible change in a repeat
  spectrum means damage, reversible shift means heating.

## Objective NA, focus and polarization
- A tightly focused beam has longitudinal (out-of-plane) field components that can excite modes forbidden for
  purely in-plane fields (Grosche et al. 2020, Opt. Express, doi 10.1364/OE.388943; arXiv 1905.12325,
  abstract). How large this leakage is for a standard 100x/0.9 objective was not quantified in what I read.
  [magnitude not verified]
- In birefringent crystals the classical Raman tensor fails because polarization changes with depth; an
  effective tensor is needed (Kranert et al. 2016, PRL 116, 127401, abstract). In thin anisotropic flakes on
  SiO2/Si, anisotropic interference changes polar patterns with thickness (Kim et al. 2015, arXiv 1510.03263).
- Si substrate intensity depends on Si crystal orientation to the laser polarization (Castellanos-Gomez 2014,
  p.8): sample/Si intensity ratios need fixed sample rotation.
- Ask whether the analyzer is fixed and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization, or the sample rotates;
  grating efficiency is polarization dependent [practice].

## Interference on SiO2/Si
- Graphene I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80,
  125422; arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Intensity ratios between bands at different shifts are
  stack-dependent.
- For MoS2 the sample intensity oscillates with thickness (interference maxima), but the ratio of sample to Si
  intensity becomes monotonic and gives thickness (Li et al. 2012, ACS Nano 6, 7381; arXiv 1308.3835,
  abstract, Fig. 4). Interference also changes optical contrast (Gorbachev et al. 2011, arXiv 1008.2868).

## Encapsulation and overlayers
- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and changes doping (Neumann et
  al. 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, p.2); it narrows BP lines and reveals a surface mode (Urban et al., arXiv
  1711.08294, abstract). Compare encapsulated with encapsulated only.
- Overlayer lines can overlap sample lines: hBN E2g near 1366 cm-1 on graphene D (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat.
  Commun. 9, 5387, p.6, via Lit-RAG). Measure an overlayer-only reference spot.

## Low-frequency modes and filters
- Shear and breathing modes (tens of cm-1) need notch or Bragg filters reaching about 5 to 10 cm-1 and
  plasma-line cleanup (Zhang 2013, p.2). Many production spectrometers cut above the graphene C mode, so absence
  below the cutoff is not evidence (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.2). Odd and even layer numbers scale differently
  (Zhang 2013, abstract).

## Spikes, plasma lines, fluorescence, baseline
- Spikes and plasma lines: see ../artifacts.md (sources listed there, not re-verified here).

Numbers only where read in the cited source (locator in brackets). [practice] marks common laboratory
practice that I could not tie to a source read for this note; treat it as advice, not evidence. Material
specifics are in graphene.md, hBN.md, black-phosphorus.md; spectrum-level artifacts also in ../artifacts.md.

## Calibration and spectral accuracy
- A first-order (linear) pixel-to-wavelength calibration of a single-grating spectrograph gave Raman shift
  errors of 5.0 to -6.8 cm-1 across the detector; with only 3 Hg lines, up to 18 cm-1; adding the quadratic
  term brought it within +-0.3 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024; arXiv 1209.0234, Methods p.10).
  Their check: graphite G 1581.5 +- 0.3 cm-1 over 12 spots.
- The error depends on where on the detector a line falls, so a single Si-line check near 520 cm-1 does not
  validate a 2D band near 2700 cm-1 [inference from the same mechanism].
- Si first order is quoted as 520 (Lee et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695; arXiv 1005.2509) and 520.9 cm-1
  (Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014, arXiv 1403.0499, p.7) in different setups: small offsets between labs are
  normal, so compare shifts relative to an internal reference measured in the same session.

## Resolution, grating and instrument line shape
- Measure resolution from the Rayleigh line: 1.9 vs 9.4 cm-1 on two instruments in one study; spectra then fit
  with Voigt profiles and the Lorentzian FWHM taken as the lifetime width (Das et al. 2008, Nat. Nanotechnol.
  3, 210; arXiv 0709.1174, p.2). About 0.6 cm-1 with a triple-filter low-frequency setup (Zhang et al. 2013,
  PRB 87, 115413; arXiv 1212.6796, p.2); 2.7 cm-1 in Lee 2010 (docs/verified-reference-numbers.md).
- Widths near the resolution (hBN 3 to 9 cm-1, BP Ag2 3 to 7 cm-1; see material notes) are instrument-limited:
  never compare raw FWHM across setups without the resolution. A 0.5 cm-1 resolution was not enough to count BP
  layers from positions (Castellanos-Gomez 2014, p.8).

## Laser heating, power density and photodamage
- Do a power series: Ferrari et al. 2006 saw no change from about 4 to 0.04 mW at 100x (arXiv
  cond-mat/0606284, p.2); typical working powers 1 mW with about 1 um spot (Cancado et al. 2011, arXiv
  1105.0175, p.2), 0.23 mW (Zhang 2013, p.2), below 300 uW at 0.5 NA (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358,
  p.7). Quote power density, not power: the same mW gives different heating at different NA.
- Temperature coefficients depend on support: graphene 2D -0.034 cm-1/K supported vs -0.072 suspended
  (Calizo 2007, arXiv 0708.1223, Table I; Chen et al. via Lee et al. 2011, arXiv 1103.3337, p.2). Do not
  convert a shift into a temperature with a coefficient from a different geometry.
- Optothermal estimates need a peak-vs-T calibration, the absorbed (not incident) power, and a measured spot
  size; using two spot sizes helps (Malekpour and Balandin 2018, J. Raman Spectrosc. 49, 106; arXiv
  1710.09749, pp.4, 18).
- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry fails under resonance when incident and scattered windows differ (Ferrari
  and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12).
- Photodamage is dose-dependent: BP oxidation rate scales with fluence (Favron et al. 2015, arXiv 1408.0345,
  p.7); MnPS3 degraded at about 50 uW when one spot was illuminated 500 s or longer (Lim et al. 2021, Curr.
  Appl. Phys. 21, 1; doi 10.1016/j.cap.2020.09.017, pp.6-7, via Lit-RAG). Irreversible change in a repeat
  spectrum means damage, reversible shift means heating.

## Objective NA, focus and polarization
- A tightly focused beam has longitudinal (out-of-plane) field components that can excite modes forbidden for
  purely in-plane fields (Grosche et al. 2020, Opt. Express, doi 10.1364/OE.388943; arXiv 1905.12325,
  abstract). How large this leakage is for a standard 100x/0.9 objective was not quantified in what I read.
  [magnitude not verified]
- In birefringent crystals the classical Raman tensor fails because polarization changes with depth; an
  effective tensor is needed (Kranert et al. 2016, PRL 116, 127401, abstract). In thin anisotropic flakes on
  SiO2/Si, anisotropic interference changes polar patterns with thickness (Kim et al. 2015, arXiv 1510.03263).
- Si substrate intensity depends on Si crystal orientation to the laser polarization (Castellanos-Gomez 2014,
  p.8): sample/Si intensity ratios need fixed sample rotation.
- Ask whether the analyzer is fixed and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization, or the sample rotates;
  grating efficiency is polarization dependent [practice].

## Interference on SiO2/Si
- Graphene I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80,
  125422; arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Intensity ratios between bands at different shifts are
  stack-dependent.
- For MoS2 the sample intensity oscillates with thickness (interference maxima), but the ratio of sample to Si
  intensity becomes monotonic and gives thickness (Li et al. 2012, ACS Nano 6, 7381; arXiv 1308.3835,
  abstract, Fig. 4). Interference also changes optical contrast (Gorbachev et al. 2011, arXiv 1008.2868).

## Encapsulation and overlayers
- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and changes doping (Neumann et
  al. 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, p.2); it narrows BP lines and reveals a surface mode (Urban et al., arXiv
  1711.08294, abstract). Compare encapsulated with encapsulated only.
- Overlayer lines can overlap sample lines: hBN E2g near 1366 cm-1 on graphene D (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat.
  Commun. 9, 5387, p.6, via Lit-RAG). Measure an overlayer-only reference spot.

## Low-frequency modes and filters
- Shear and breathing modes (tens of cm-1) need notch or Bragg filters reaching about 5 to 10 cm-1 and
  plasma-line cleanup (Zhang 2013, p.2). Many production spectrometers cut above the graphene C mode, so absence
  below the cutoff is not evidence (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.2). Odd and even layer numbers scale differently
  (Zhang 2013, abstract).

## Spikes, plasma lines, fluorescence, baseline
- Spikes and plasma lines: see ../artifacts.md (sources listed there, not re-verified here).

input.summary: Raman can't confirm that flake 2 is a monolayer. It shows that flake 2 is a much thinner hBN flake than flake 1, and that is all it shows. The E2g line is real (S/N about 14) and weak, and its area is about 0.10 of flake 1's. Against the Si 520 line it is about 190 times weaker. The line sits at 1369.0 ± 0.3 cm-1, about 2.8 cm-1 above flake 1, and is broad. All of that fits a few-layer or monolayer flake on SiO2/Si. A shift of that size also appears in 2L and sometimes 3L, and strain can produce it. The data do not include a flake-1 thickness or a known 1L reference, so intensity cannot be turned into a layer count. My reading is that flake 2 is thin, at most a few layers, with a monolayer plausible but unproven. AFM or a calibrated optical contrast would decide it.

observations.finding: Flake 1 shows the strong, bulk-like hBN E2g band; its position matches bulk hBN within the quoted scatter.
observations.evidence: Lorentzian + linear background fit, 1250-1500 cm-1 window: centre 1366.19 ± 0.04 cm-1, FWHM 18.0 ± 0.1 cm-1, height 3232 ± 13 counts above a baseline of about 1150 (S/N about 80), area about 9.2e4. Bulk reference 1366.6 ± 0.2 cm-1.
observations.source: Bulk value: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656), p.7

observations.finding: Flake 2 shows a weak but real E2g band that is up-shifted and broader than flake 1.
observations.evidence: Same fit: centre 1368.99 ± 0.23 cm-1, FWHM 21.6 ± 0.8 cm-1, height 269 ± 6 counts on a baseline of about 1570 counts (S/N about 14), area about 9.2e3. rl_series gives the same shift, +2.84 ± 0.25 cm-1 versus flake 1 (fit error only).

observations.finding: The up-shift is not a calibration artifact.
observations.evidence: The Si first-order line is at 520.93 cm-1 in flake 1 and 520.90 cm-1 in flake 2 (offsets +0.23 and +0.20 from 520.7). They differ by about 0.03 cm-1 and are equally offset, so a +2.8 cm-1 hBN shift exceeds the combined calibration and fit uncertainty of about 0.3-0.5 cm-1. Both spectra have a similar point spacing of about 0.75 cm-1.

observations.finding: Flake 2 is far thinner than flake 1, judged by the hBN-to-substrate intensity ratio. The size of the ratio is stack-dependent, so it is only semi-quantitative.
observations.evidence: Raw E2g area ratio flake2/flake1 is about 0.10. Normalised to the Si 520 area, hBN/Si is 17.4 for flake 1 and 0.092 for flake 2, a factor of about 190. In flake 2 the Si 520 peak (about 18000 counts) and the Si second-order band near 950-980 cm-1 (about 285 counts, bands at 950.6 and 979.5) are strong and about as large as the hBN line. In flake 1 the Si 520 peak is only about 980 counts and the 2TO band is not visible. The 18-fold difference in Si signal between the flakes means the optical coupling differs strongly (interference through the oxide plus hBN, or focus), so the raw 10x and the Si-normalised 190x bracket the true ratio.

observations.finding: Integrated E2g intensity scales with layer number on a given substrate, so in principle it separates 1L, 2L and thicker flakes. It needs a calibration flake of known N, which is not available here.
observations.evidence: Flake 1 has no independent thickness. If it is tens of nm thick (hundreds of layers), a 0.1 ratio would put flake 2 at about 10-30 layers on the raw ratio. The Si-normalised ratio would imply an order of magnitude fewer. The estimate is therefore unconstrained between about 1 and about 30 layers without flake 1's thickness.
observations.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465 (arXiv 1008.2868), p.4, Fig. 4a inset

observations.finding: The positional up-shift fits thin hBN on SiO2, but position is not a layer-number test.
observations.evidence: Substrate-supported 1L 1369.6 ± 0.6, 2L 1369.0 ± 0.5, 3L 1367.5 ± 0.2 cm-1; flake 2 at 1369.0 ± 0.3 matches 1L or 2L and is about 1.5 cm-1 above 3L. Gorbachev reports 1L shifted up 2-4 cm-1 and 2L usually down 1-2 cm-1. The two papers disagree, and Cai attributes the shifts mainly to substrate strain. Heating would lower, not raise, the frequency, so it does not explain the up-shift.
observations.source: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656), pp.7-8, Fig. 1; Gorbachev et al. 2011 (arXiv 1008.2868), pp.1, 4, Fig. 4b

observations.finding: The width increase from 18.0 to 21.6 cm-1 is consistent with thin flakes and strain inhomogeneity. It is not a clean defect metric, because the instrument and the isotope floor limit the interpretation.
observations.evidence: FWHM 18.0 ± 0.1 (flake 1) versus 21.6 ± 0.8 (flake 2). Si 520 FWHM is about 3.4-3.5 cm-1, so the instrument contribution is small compared with these widths. The literature widths for bulk are quoted inconsistently (HWHM about 9 versus FWHM about 9). The 1L HWHM is 10-12 versus about 9 bulk, a roughly 20 % increase, similar to what is seen here.
observations.source: Gorbachev 2011, p.4; Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387, p.6

observations.finding: The small feature at 1474.6 cm-1 reported by the series tool in flake 2 is noise and not a mode.
observations.evidence: In the raw data the points near 1474 cm-1 reach about 1599 counts against a local median of 1552 and a noise sd of about 19 counts, so at most about 2.5 sigma and a single point. The fit width is 3.4 ± 5.5 cm-1.

observations.finding: The rest of the flake 2 spectrum is the Si substrate: the broad doublet at about 950 and 980 cm-1 is Si second-order.
observations.evidence: Bands at 950.58 ± 0.41 and 979.48 ± 0.38 cm-1 (FWHM about 17-19 cm-1) in flake 2. They are expected from Si 2TO and are not hBN features. No other hBN band is expected in 450-1650 cm-1 apart from E2g.
observations.source: Si second-order near 950-980 cm-1: raman-analysis QC notes (rl_qc.py)

properties.name: layers
properties.value: Not determined. Thin, at most a few layers (monolayer plausible, 2L-3L equally possible); not a bulk flake like flake 1.
properties.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011 (arXiv 1008.2868) Fig. 4a; Cai et al. 2017 (arXiv 2008.01656) Fig. 1

properties.name: strain_sign
properties.value: Likely tensile or compressive substrate-induced strain cannot be separated; E2g is up-shifted +2.8 ± 0.3 cm-1 relative to flake 1 (the sign of strain cannot be assigned without a strain-free reference and the Gruneisen parameter, which I did not use).
properties.source: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059, pp.13-16, Fig. 4

properties.name: doping_type
properties.value: none (insulator; doping is not an expected explanation)
properties.source: Cai et al. 2017, p.7

properties.name: defect_level
properties.value: Not determinable; no sourced Raman defect marker for hBN beyond width, and widths are confounded by thickness, strain and isotope floor
properties.source: hBN reading notes (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358, pp.3, 7)

caveats: Absolute intensity, and also the hBN/Si ratio, depends on interference in the 290 nm SiO2 plus hBN stack and on focus. The 18-fold lower Si 520 intensity on flake 1 versus flake 2 shows how different the two optical situations are, so a single ratio is not a thickness.

Position alone cannot give layer number: the 1L and 2L supported values (1369.6 ± 0.6 and 1369.0 ± 0.5) overlap with each other, and strain from substrate roughness (or thermal mismatch if the flake was annealed) can produce a 1-4 cm-1 up-shift in any thin flake. The two literature sources disagree on whether position tracks N at all.

Optical invisibility argues for a thin flake but not strictly for 1L: 1L contrast on SiO2 is under 1.5 % in white light, and the contrast is wavelength- and oxide-dependent (sign change near 530 nm), so a few-layer flake could also look faint. Contamination, polymer residue or a tape-residue film could also be faint.

The flake 2 peak was fitted with a single Lorentzian on a linear baseline above a Si-dominated, higher background (about 1570 versus about 1150 counts); the position error of 0.23 cm-1 is a fit statistic, and the true uncertainty is closer to 0.3-0.5 cm-1 once calibration is included. Spot size larger than the flake would also dilute the hBN intensity and make a larger flake look thinner.
The data start at 450 cm-1, so the shear mode near 50 cm-1 (which would give a clean layer-number count) was not measured; its absence is not evidence.
Flake 1 thickness is unknown, so the 'about 10-30 layers' scaling estimate is only illustrative.

Power, integration time and objective NA are said to be equal but not given, so heating and spot-size comparisons are assumed equal; heating would lower the frequency, so it cannot explain the up-shift.
questions_for_user: What is the thickness of flake 1 (AFM or optical contrast), and was a known 1L or 2L hBN flake ever measured on the same substrate? That gives the intensity calibration that turns a Raman area ratio into a layer count.
Were both flakes on the same chip, and was flake 2 annealed or transferred (strain and wrinkles shift E2g by several cm-1)?
What are the laser power density, objective/NA, spot size, and the real spectral resolution? They set the broadening and the heating, and whether flake 2 fills the spot.

What is the isotope content and source crystal (natural B gives about 7.5-8 cm-1 FWHM floor)? The measured widths of 18-22 cm-1 are much larger than that, so is that width instrumental or fitted differently?
Can you measure the low-frequency shear mode near 50 cm-1 on flake 2 with a notch/Bragg setup? Its presence or absence directly separates 1L from 2L and more.
Can you acquire an optical-contrast (green channel) or AFM height map for flake 2? A step of about 0.33-0.4 nm per layer is the direct test.
citations: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465 (arXiv 1008.2868): Fig. 4a (intensity vs N), Fig. 4b (position vs N), pp.1-4.
Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656): Fig. 1 (supported vs suspended positions), Fig. 4 (annealing), pp.7-8, 13-16.
Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387, p.6 (bulk FWHM about 9 cm-1; no dispersion with laser energy).
Janzen et al. 2023 (arXiv 2306.13358), pp.3, 7 (isotope width floor, shear mode).
Local reference notes: reference/materials/hBN.md and general-measurement.md in the ramanlens raman-analysis skill (consulted for the above).
limits: Raman at 514.5 nm on a single spot cannot assign an absolute layer number to hBN without an intensity calibration standard, an independent thickness measurement (AFM), or low-frequency shear-mode data.

The measured position (1369.0 ± 0.3 cm-1) and width are consistent with 1L, 2L and strained thin flakes, so the data cannot discriminate between them; I did not evaluate a strain Gruneisen relation, so no strain value is reported.
Defect density, doping and temperature effects are not constrained by these spectra: no sourced defect band exists for hBN, and heating would give the opposite shift sign.

Monolayer vs bilayer vs few-layer is the question; I can only say 'thin, with a monolayer not excluded'. I did not run a CRD/library match because the material is stated and only E2g is observable in this window.
Spectra start at 450 cm-1 and end at 1650 cm-1, so nothing about shear modes, B-N overtones or fluorescence beyond this range is known.

caveats: Absolute intensity, and also the hBN/Si ratio, depends on interference in the 290 nm SiO2 plus hBN stack and on focus. The 18-fold lower Si 520 intensity on flake 1 versus flake 2 shows how different the two optical situations are, so a single ratio is not a thickness.

Position alone cannot give layer number: the 1L and 2L supported values (1369.6 ± 0.6 and 1369.0 ± 0.5) overlap with each other, and strain from substrate roughness (or thermal mismatch if the flake was annealed) can produce a 1-4 cm-1 up-shift in any thin flake. The two literature sources disagree on whether position tracks N at all.

Optical invisibility argues for a thin flake but not strictly for 1L: 1L contrast on SiO2 is under 1.5 % in white light, and the contrast is wavelength- and oxide-dependent (sign change near 530 nm), so a few-layer flake could also look faint. The flake 2 peak was fitted with a single Lorentzian on a linear baseline above a Si-dominated, higher background (about 1570 versus about 1150 counts); the position error of 0.23 cm-1 is a fit statistic, and the true uncertainty is closer to 0.3-0.5 cm-1 once calibration is included. Spot size larger than the flake would also dilute the hBN intensity and make a larger flake look thinner.
The data start at 450 cm-1, so the shear mode near 50 cm-1 (which would give a clean layer-number count) was not measured; its absence is not evidence.
Flake 1 thickness is unknown, so the 'about 10-30 layers' scaling estimate is only illustrative.

Power, integration time and objective NA are said to be equal but not given, so heating and spot-size comparisons are assumed equal; heating would lower the frequency, so it cannot explain the up-shift.
questions_for_user: What is the thickness of flake 1 (AFM or optical contrast), and was a known 1L or 2L hBN flake ever measured on the same substrate? That gives the intensity calibration that turns a Raman area ratio into a layer count.
Were both flakes on the same chip, and was flake 2 annealed or transferred (strain and wrinkles shift E2g by several cm-1)?
What are the laser power density, objective/NA, spot size, and the real spectral resolution? They set the broadening and the heating, and whether flake 2 fills the spot.

What is the isotope content and source crystal (natural B gives about 7.5-8 cm-1 FWHM floor)? The measured widths of 18-22 cm-1 are much larger than that, so is that width instrumental or fitted differently?
Can you measure the low-frequency shear mode near 50 cm-1 on flake 2 with a notch/Bragg setup? Its presence or absence directly separates 1L from 2L and more.
Can you acquire an optical-contrast (green channel) or AFM height map for flake 2? A step of about 0.33-0.4 nm per layer is the direct test.

Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656): Fig. 1 (supported vs suspended positions), Fig. 4 (annealing), pp.7-8, 13-16.
Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387, p.6 (bulk FWHM about 9 cm-1; no dispersion with laser energy).

limits: Raman at 514.5 nm on a single spot cannot assign an absolute layer number to hBN without an intensity calibration standard, an independent thickness measurement (AFM), or low-frequency shear-mode data.

The measured position (1369.0 ± 0.3 cm-1) and width are consistent with 1L, 2L and strained thin flakes, so the data cannot discriminate between them; I did not evaluate a strain Gruneisen relation, so no strain value is reported.
Defect density, doping and temperature effects are not constrained by these spectra: no sourced defect band exists for hBN, and heating would give the opposite shift sign.

Monolayer vs bilayer vs few-layer is the question; I can only say 'thin, with a monolayer not excluded'. I did not run a CRD/library match because the material is stated and only E2g is observable in this window.
Spectra start at 450 cm-1 and end at 1650 cm-1, so nothing about shear modes, B-N overtones or fluorescence beyond this range is known.

observations.finding: Flake 2 shows a weak but real E2g band that is up-shifted and broader than flake 1.

structured_output.summary: Raman can't confirm that flake 2 is a monolayer. It shows that flake 2 is a much thinner hBN flake than flake 1, and that is all it shows. The E2g line is real (S/N about 14) and weak, and its area is about 0.10 of flake 1's. Against the Si 520 line it is about 190 times weaker. The line sits at 1369.0 ± 0.3 cm-1, about 2.8 cm-1 above flake 1, and is broad. All of that fits a few-layer or monolayer flake on SiO2/Si. A shift of that size also appears in 2L and sometimes 3L, and strain can produce it. The data do not include a flake-1 thickness or a known 1L reference, so intensity cannot be turned into a layer count. My reading is that flake 2 is thin, at most a few layers, with a monolayer plausible but unproven. AFM or a calibrated optical contrast would decide it.

observations.finding: Flake 1 shows the strong, bulk-like hBN E2g band; its position matches bulk hBN within the quoted scatter.
observations.evidence: Lorentzian + linear background fit, 1250-1500 cm-1 window: centre 1366.19 ± 0.04 cm-1, FWHM 18.0 ± 0.1 cm-1, height 3232 ± 13 counts above a baseline of about 1150 (S/N about 80), area about 9.2e4. Bulk reference 1366.6 ± 0.2 cm-1.
observations.source: Bulk value: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656), p.7

observations.finding: Flake 2 shows a weak but real E2g band that is up-shifted and broader than flake 1.
observations.evidence: Same fit: centre 1368.99 ± 0.23 cm-1, FWHM 21.6 ± 0.8 cm-1, height 269 ± 6 counts on a baseline of about 1570 counts (S/N about 14), area about 9.2e3. rl_series gives the same shift, +2.84 ± 0.25 cm-1 versus flake 1 (fit error only).

observations.finding: The up-shift is not a calibration artifact.
observations.evidence: The Si first-order line is at 520.93 cm-1 in flake 1 and 520.90 cm-1 in flake 2 (offsets +0.23 and +0.20 from 520.7). They differ by about 0.03 cm-1 and are equally offset, so a +2.8 cm-1 hBN shift exceeds the combined calibration and fit uncertainty of about 0.3-0.5 cm-1. Both spectra have a similar point spacing of about 0.75 cm-1.

observations.finding: Flake 2 is far thinner than flake 1, judged by the hBN-to-substrate intensity ratio. The size of the ratio is stack-dependent, so it is only semi-quantitative.
observations.evidence: Raw E2g area ratio flake2/flake1 is about 0.10. Normalised to the Si 520 area, hBN/Si is 17.4 for flake 1 and 0.092 for flake 2, a factor of about 190. In flake 2 the Si 520 peak (about 18000 counts) and the Si second-order band near 950-980 cm-1 (about 285 counts, bands at 950.6 and 979.5) are strong and about as large as the hBN line. In flake 1 the Si 520 peak is only about 980 counts and the 2TO band is not visible. The 18-fold difference in Si signal between the flakes means the optical coupling differs strongly (interference through the oxide plus hBN, or focus), so the raw 10x and the Si-normalised 190x bracket the true ratio.

observations.finding: Integrated E2g intensity scales with layer number on a given substrate, so in principle it separates 1L, 2L and thicker flakes. It needs a calibration flake of known N, which is not available here.
observations.evidence: Flake 1 has no independent thickness. If it is tens of nm thick (hundreds of layers), a 0.1 ratio would put flake 2 at about 10-30 layers on the raw ratio. The Si-normalised ratio would imply an order of magnitude fewer. The estimate is therefore unconstrained between about 1 and about 30 layers without flake 1's thickness.
observations.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465 (arXiv 1008.2868), p.4, Fig. 4a inset

observations.finding: The positional up-shift fits thin hBN on SiO2, but position is not a layer-number test.
observations.evidence: Substrate-supported 1L 1369.6 ± 0.6, 2L 1369.0 ± 0.5, 3L 1367.5 ± 0.2 cm-1; flake 2 at 1369.0 ± 0.3 matches 1L or 2L and is about 1.5 cm-1 above 3L. Gorbachev reports 1L shifted up 2-4 cm-1 and 2L usually down 1-2 cm-1. The two papers disagree, and Cai attributes the shifts mainly to substrate strain. Heating would lower, not raise, the frequency, so it does not explain the up-shift.
observations.source: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656), pp.7-8, Fig. 1; Gorbachev et al. 2011 (arXiv 1008.2868), pp.1, 4, Fig. 4b

observations.finding: The width increase from 18.0 to 21.6 cm-1 is consistent with thin flakes and strain inhomogeneity. It is not a clean defect metric, because the instrument and the isotope floor limit the interpretation.
observations.evidence: FWHM 18.0 ± 0.1 (flake 1) versus 21.6 ± 0.8 (flake 2). Si 520 FWHM is about 3.4-3.5 cm-1, so the instrument contribution is small compared with these widths. The literature widths for bulk are quoted inconsistently (HWHM about 9 versus FWHM about 9). The 1L HWHM is 10-12 versus about 9 bulk, a roughly 20 % increase, similar to what is seen here.
observations.source: Gorbachev 2011, p.4; Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387, p.6

observations.finding: The small feature at 1474.6 cm-1 reported by the series tool in flake 2 is noise and not a mode.
observations.evidence: In the raw data the points near 1474 cm-1 reach about 1599 counts against a local median of 1552 and a noise sd of about 19 counts, so at most about 2.5 sigma and a single point. The fit width is 3.4 ± 5.5 cm-1.

observations.finding: The rest of the flake 2 spectrum is the Si substrate: the broad doublet at about 950 and 980 cm-1 is Si second-order.
observations.evidence: Bands at 950.58 ± 0.41 and 979.48 ± 0.38 cm-1 (FWHM about 17-19 cm-1) in flake 2. They are expected from Si 2TO and are not hBN features. No other hBN band is expected in 450-1650 cm-1 apart from E2g.
observations.source: Si second-order near 950-980 cm-1: raman-analysis QC notes (rl_qc.py)

properties.name: layers
properties.value: Not determined. Thin, at most a few layers (monolayer plausible, 2L-3L equally possible); not a bulk flake like flake 1.
properties.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011 (arXiv 1008.2868) Fig. 4a; Cai et al. 2017 (arXiv 2008.01656) Fig. 1

properties.name: strain_sign
properties.value: Cannot be assigned. E2g is up-shifted +2.8 ± 0.3 cm-1 relative to flake 1, but strain cannot be separated from a thickness effect without a strain-free reference and the Gruneisen parameter, which I did not use.
properties.source: Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059, pp.13-16, Fig. 4

properties.name: doping_type
properties.value: none (insulator; doping is not an expected explanation)
properties.source: Cai et al. 2017, p.7

properties.name: defect_level
properties.value: Not determinable; no sourced Raman defect marker for hBN beyond width, and widths are confounded by thickness, strain and isotope floor
properties.source: hBN reading notes (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358, pp.3, 7)

caveats: Absolute intensity, and also the hBN/Si ratio, depends on interference in the 290 nm SiO2 plus hBN stack and on focus. The 18-fold lower Si 520 intensity on flake 1 versus flake 2 shows how different the two optical situations are, so a single ratio is not a thickness.

Position alone cannot give layer number: the 1L and 2L supported values (1369.6 ± 0.6 and 1369.0 ± 0.5) overlap with each other, and strain from substrate roughness (or thermal mismatch if the flake was annealed) can produce a 1-4 cm-1 up-shift in any thin flake. The two literature sources disagree on whether position tracks N at all.

Optical invisibility argues for a thin flake but not strictly for 1L: 1L contrast on SiO2 is under 1.5 % in white light, and the contrast is wavelength- and oxide-dependent (sign change near 530 nm), so a few-layer flake could also look faint. Contamination, polymer residue or a tape-residue film could also be faint.

The flake 2 peak was fitted with a single Lorentzian on a linear baseline above a Si-dominated, higher background (about 1570 versus about 1150 counts); the position error of 0.23 cm-1 is a fit statistic, and the true uncertainty is closer to 0.3-0.5 cm-1 once calibration is included. Spot size larger than the flake would also dilute the hBN intensity and make a larger flake look thinner.
The data start at 450 cm-1, so the shear mode near 50 cm-1 (which would give a clean layer-number count) was not measured; its absence is not evidence.
Flake 1 thickness is unknown, so the 'about 10-30 layers' scaling estimate is only illustrative.

Power, integration time and objective NA are said to be equal but not given, so heating and spot-size comparisons are assumed equal; heating would lower the frequency, so it cannot explain the up-shift.
questions_for_user: What is the thickness of flake 1 (AFM or optical contrast), and was a known 1L or 2L hBN flake ever measured on the same substrate? That gives the intensity calibration that turns a Raman area ratio into a layer count.
Were both flakes on the same chip, and was flake 2 annealed or transferred (strain and wrinkles shift E2g by several cm-1)?
What are the laser power density, objective/NA, spot size, and the real spectral resolution? They set the broadening and the heating, and whether flake 2 fills the spot.

What is the isotope content and source crystal (natural B gives about 7.5-8 cm-1 FWHM floor)? The measured widths of 18-22 cm-1 are much larger than that, so is that width instrumental or fitted differently?
Can you measure the low-frequency shear mode near 50 cm-1 on flake 2 with a notch/Bragg setup? Its presence or absence directly separates 1L from 2L and more.
Can you acquire an optical-contrast (green channel) or AFM height map for flake 2? A step of about 0.33-0.4 nm per layer is the direct test.

Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656): Fig. 1 (supported vs suspended positions), Fig. 4 (annealing), pp.7-8, 13-16.
Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387, p.6 (bulk FWHM about 9 cm-1; no dispersion with laser energy).
Janzen et al. 2023 (arXiv 2306.13358), pp.3, 7 (isotope width floor, shear mode).
Local reference notes: reference/materials/hBN.md and general-measurement.md in the ramanlens raman-analysis skill (consulted for the above).
limits: Raman at 514.5 nm on a single spot cannot assign an absolute layer number to hBN without an intensity calibration standard, an independent thickness measurement (AFM), or low-frequency shear-mode data.

The measured position (1369.0 ± 0.3 cm-1) and width are consistent with 1L, 2L and strained thin flakes, so the data cannot discriminate between them; I did not evaluate a strain Gruneisen relation, so no strain value is reported.
Defect density, doping and temperature effects are not constrained by these spectra: no sourced defect band exists for hBN, and heating would give the opposite shift sign.

Monolayer vs bilayer vs few-layer is the question; I can only say 'thin, with a monolayer not excluded'. I did not run a CRD/library match because the material is stated and only E2g is observable in this window.
Spectra start at 450 cm-1 and end at 1650 cm-1, so nothing about shear modes, B-N overtones or fluorescence beyond this range is known.
